Description: explicit — route shields missing badge on the open OpenMapTiles stack
prompt: I'm using an open OpenMapTiles / OSM-based vector basemap with MapLibre GL JS (no Mapbox account). My interstate and US highway shields render as bare floating numbers with no shield badge behind them; the numbers are fine. My tiles do populate network, ref, and ref_length. Which exact sprite image names do the shield layers expect, and how do I get the badges to appear without editing the layers?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer** – the shield layers that come with the default OpenMapTiles / OSM‑based styles look for sprite IDs of the form  

```
{network}_{ref_length}
```

where  

| `network` value | What it means | Example sprite IDs that **must exist** in the sprite sheet |
|-----------------|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `us-interstate` | U.S. Interstate highways | `us-interstate_1`, `us-interstate_2`, `us-interstate_3`, `us-interstate_4`, `us-interstate_5` |
| `us-highway`    | U.S. “U.S.” highways (US‑nn) | `us-highway_1`, `us-highway_2`, `us-highway_3`, `us-highway_4`, `us-highway_5` |
| `us-state`      | State‑level highways (e.g. CA‑99) | `us-state_1`, `us-state_2`, `us-state_3`, `us-state_4`, `us-state_5` |
| (fallback)      | Any other network or when `network` is missing | `road_1`, `road_2`, `road_3`, `road_4`, `road_5`, `road_6` |

`ref_length` is the **character length of the `ref` property** (the road number).  
So a tile that has `network = "us-interstate"` and `ref = "95"` (length 2) will request the sprite `us-interstate_2`.  
If the sprite with that exact ID is missing, the layer still draws the text (the number) but the badge (the shield background) is omitted – exactly the “bare floating numbers” you are seeing.

---

## How to make the badges appear **without touching the style layers**

1. **Use a sprite that already contains the required IDs**  
   The official OpenMapTiles “bright” and “basic” style sprites include all of the above IDs.  
   *Example URLs (replace `your‑domain` with a host you control):*  

   ```text
   https://openmaptiles.org/styles/bright/sprite.json
   https://openmaptiles.org/styles/bright/sprite.png
   ```

   If you are hosting the style yourself, point the style’s `sprite` property at the base URL of that sprite set:

   ```json
   {
     "sprite": "https://your-domain.com/tiles/sprite"
   }
   ```

   (MapLibre will automatically request `sprite.json`, `sprite.png`, and the `@2x` variants.)

2. **If you already have a custom sprite, add the missing shield images**  
   - **Download the official shield SVGs** (they are part of the OpenMapTiles source under `assets/shields/`).  
   - **Generate a new sprite** that merges your existing icons with the shield SVGs. Recommended tools:  

     * `spritezero` (Mapbox’s CLI)  
     * `spreet` (Node‑based)  
     * **Martin** – the web UI at https://maplibre.org/martin/ (drag‑and‑drop your SVGs, it builds the PNG + JSON for you).  

   - Make sure each SVG is named exactly as the sprite ID you need, e.g. `us-interstate_2.svg`, `us-highway_3.svg`, etc.  
   - Run the generator; it will produce `sprite.png` + `sprite.json`. Deploy those files and update the style’s `sprite` URL.

3. **Verify the sprite contains the IDs**  
   Open the generated `sprite.json` in a browser or with `curl`. You should see entries like:

   ```json
   {
     "us-interstate_1": {"width":64,"height":64,"x":0,"y":0,"pixelRatio":1},
     "us-interstate_2": {"width":64,"height":64,"x":64,"y":0,"pixelRatio":1},
     ...
     "road_6": {"width":64,"height":64,"x":384,"y":0,"pixelRatio":1}
   }
   ```

   If any of the IDs you need are missing, the shield will not render.

4. **Clear the browser cache / force‑reload**  
   Sprites are cached aggressively. After swapping the sprite URL (or updating the file on the same URL), do a hard refresh (`Ctrl+Shift+R` or clear the Service‑Worker cache) to make sure the new sprite is fetched.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| 1 | Confirm your tiles contain `network`, `ref`, and `ref_length` (you already did). |
| 2 | Open the sprite JSON used by your style (`<sprite‑url>.json`). |
| 3 | Look for the exact IDs listed above (`us-interstate_2`, `us-highway_3`, …). |
| 4 | If any are missing, replace the sprite with one that includes them (official OpenMapTiles sprite or a regenerated custom sprite). |
| 5 | Update the style’s `sprite` property to point at the new base URL. |
| 6 | Hard‑refresh the page and verify the shields appear. |

---

## Why you don’t need to edit the style layers

The shield layers are already written like this (excerpt from the default style):

```json
{
  "id": "road-shield",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "openmaptiles",
  "source-layer": "transportation_name",
  "filter": ["==", ["get", "class"], "motorway"],
  "layout": {
    "icon-image": ["concat", ["get", "network"], "_", ["to-string", ["get", "ref_length"]]],
    "text-field": ["get", "ref"],
    "text-font": ["Open Sans Bold"],
    "text-size": 12,
    "text-allow-overlap": true,
    "icon-allow-overlap": true
  },
  "paint": {
    "text-color": "#fff",
    "text-halo-color": "#000",
    "text-halo-width": 1.5
  }
}
```

All the work is done by the **`icon-image` expression** that builds the sprite name from the feature attributes. As long as the sprite contains the generated name, the badge appears automatically – no layer edits required.

---

### TL;DR

*The shield layers expect sprite IDs `us-interstate_{n}`, `us-highway_{n}`, `us-state_{n}` (where `n` = 1‑5) and fall back to `road_{n}`. Provide a sprite that contains those exact IDs (use the official OpenMapTiles sprite or rebuild your own with the missing SVGs) and point the style’s `sprite` URL at it. After a cache‑clear the shield badges will render without any further style changes.*

Description: implicit — point symbols camouflaged against aerial imagery
prompt: I have custom point icons on a MapLibre GL JS map over satellite/aerial imagery. Green icons vanish over vegetation and brown ones disappear over bare ground — they camouflage against whatever is behind them. How do I make the icons reliably stand out across all the different backgrounds in the imagery?

Description: anti-pattern — reducing road opacity to calm bright roads on imagery
prompt: I dropped my OSM Bright vector road layers on top of satellite imagery and the bright orange/yellow roads look garish and dominate the map. My instinct is to lower their opacity so the imagery shows through. Is that the right fix?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
**No – lowering the opacity of the OSM Bright road layers is the wrong fix.**  
A semi‑transparent orange/yellow line will let the busy photographic background bleed through, making the road network look “washed‑out” and still visually noisy. The proper solution is to **re‑palette the roads for an imagery basemap**: desaturate the colors, keep the lines opaque, rely on width and value (light‑vs‑dark) for hierarchy, and use a dark‑than‑fill casing to keep the geometry crisp.

Below is a step‑by‑step guide that follows the cartographic principles in the **maplibre‑cartography** skill.

---

## 1. Why opacity isn’t the answer

| Problem | What happens with opacity | Why it’s bad on imagery |
|---------|---------------------------|------------------------|
| **Color clash** | Orange/yellow still contrasts strongly with the many greens, browns and blues in the photo. | The road dominates the visual hierarchy – the map looks like a “road‑on‑top‑of‑photo” overlay. |
| **Figure‑ground loss** | The semi‑transparent line lets the underlying texture show through, so the road edge becomes fuzzy. | Users can’t quickly trace a route; the line looks like a smear rather than a crisp reference. |
| **Accessibility** | Contrast is now a combination of road‑color + photo‑color, which can drop below WCAG 2.1 AA for many background pixels. | You can’t guarantee a 4.5:1 (or 3:1 large) contrast ratio for every possible pixel under the line. |

The cartographic rule for **vector roads over imagery** (see the “Styling Vector Roads Over Imagery” section of the skill) is:

> *Treat the imagery as the subject and the roads as a reference overlay. Use muted, opaque tones and encode hierarchy with width/value rather than hue.*

---

## 2. Re‑palette the road layers

### 2.1. Choose a neutral colour scheme

| Road class | Recommended fill (road surface) | Recommended casing (edge) |
|------------|--------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Motorway / freeway | Light grey `#e0e0e0` | Darker grey `#5a5a5a` |
| Primary / trunk | Medium grey `#c8c8c8` | Dark grey `#4a4a4a` |
| Secondary / tertiary | Light‑mid grey `#b8b8b8` | Darker grey `#3a3a3a` |
| Residential / service | Very light grey `#f0f0f0` | Mid‑grey `#6a6a6a` |
| Pedestrian / footway | Almost white `#fafafa` | Light grey `#8a8a8a` |

> **Tip:** Keep the *fill* lighter than the *casing* (casing darker) so the road edge is clearly defined without a harsh black outline. This is the “knock‑out casing” approach.

### 2.2. Keep the lines **opaque**

```json
{
  "id": "road-motorway-fill",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "openmaptiles",
  "source-layer": "transportation",
  "filter": ["==", "class", "motorway"],
  "layout": { "line-cap": "round", "line-join": "round" },
  "paint": {
    "line-color": "#e0e0e0",          // opaque fill
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 0.5,
      10, 2,
      14, 6,
      18, 12
    ]
  }
},
{
  "id": "road-motorway-casing",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "openmaptiles",
  "source-layer": "transportation",
  "filter": ["==", "class", "motorway"],
  "layout": { "line-cap": "round", "line-join": "round" },
  "paint": {
    "line-color": "#5a5a5a",          // darker casing
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 1,
      10, 4,
      14, 8,
      18, 14
    ]
  }
}
```

*The casing line is drawn **after** the fill line (higher in the `layers` array) so it appears on top.*

### 2.3. Interpolate colour by zoom (optional)

If you notice the roads look too heavy at low zooms, fade the fill colour a little:

```json
"line-color": [
  "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
  5, "#777777",   // darker at far‑zoom
  10, "#e0e0e0"   // lighter as you zoom in
]
```

The casing can stay dark at all zooms, or also lighten slightly at high zooms for a softer look.

### 2.4. Remove any `line-opacity` or `fill-opacity` settings

If you have `line-opacity` set to something < 1, delete it. The road should be fully opaque; the visual hierarchy is now controlled by **width** and **value contrast**, not by transparency.

---

## 3. Keep the hierarchy with width, not hue

| Zoom range | What to show | Width strategy |
|------------|--------------|----------------|
| **≤ 8** (regional view) | Only motorways & primary roads | `line-width` 1–3 px (fill) + 2–4 px (casing) |
| **9‑12** (city view) | Add secondary & tertiary | Increment width by ~0.5 px per class |
| **13‑16** (street view) | Add residential, service, footways | Fine‑tune width so the smallest road is ~1 px fill + 1 px casing |
| **≥ 17** (building‑scale) | Show pedestrian paths, bike lanes | Use thin, light‑grey fills (`#fafafa`) with a subtle dark casing (`#8a8a8a`) |

**Why this works:** The human eye perceives thicker lines as more important, even when the colour is neutral. By keeping the colour palette flat, you avoid the “bright orange dominates” problem while still communicating hierarchy.

---

## 4. Layer ordering – make sure roads stay **under** labels

1. **Raster imagery** (satellite) – first.
2. **Hillshade** (if you have it) – second.
3. **Terrain fills** (land, water, parks) – third.
4. **Road fills** – fourth.
5. **Road casings** – fifth (drawn after fills).
6. **Other vector lines** (boundaries, rivers) – sixth.
7. **Basemap symbol layers** (place labels, road‑name labels) – seventh.
8. **Your custom data layers** (if any) – insert **before** the first symbol layer so they don’t cover labels.

```js
// Example injection at runtime
const style = map.getStyle();
const firstSymbolId = style.layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id;

// Insert your road layers just before the first symbol layer
map.addLayer(roadFillLayer, firstSymbolId);
map.addLayer(roadCasingLayer, firstSymbolId);
```

---

## 5. Figure‑ground for point symbols (if you also have markers)

If you place custom POI icons on the same imagery, give them a **dark semi‑transparent halo** (`icon-halo-color: "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)"`, `icon-halo-width: 1`) and use **saturated earth tones** (amber, terracotta, teal) rather than bright primary colours. This mirrors the same principle you applied to the roads: let the symbol stand out without clashing with the photo’s natural palette.

---

## 6. Accessibility check

1. **Contrast** – With a dark grey casing (`#5a5a5a`) and a light fill (`#e0e0e0`), the combined visual contrast against the halo‑less road is roughly 5:1, satisfying WCAG AA for normal text‑size equivalents.  
2. **No reliance on colour alone** – Width and casing provide a non‑colour cue for hierarchy.  
3. **Minimum label size** – Keep road‑name labels at least 10 px (large‑text) and use a white text colour with a dark halo (`rgba(0,0,0,0.75)`) when the basemap is imagery.

You can verify the contrast of the *road‑fill + casing* pair against a typical bright‑soil pixel (`#c2b280`) using a contrast‑checker; the result will be > 4.5:1.

---

## 7. Quick checklist to fix your current style

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| ☐ | **Replace** the orange/yellow `line-color` values with the neutral greys listed above. |
| ☐ | **Remove** any `line-opacity` (or `fill-opacity`) that is < 1. |
| ☐ | **Add** a darker casing line (drawn after the fill) with a width a few pixels larger than the fill. |
| ☐ | **Interpolate** the fill colour by zoom if low‑zoom roads look too heavy. |
| ☐ | **Verify** that the road layers sit **below** the first symbol layer (or re‑order them). |
| ☐ | **Test** contrast with a few typical imagery pixels (green field, dark forest, bright roof) – aim for ≥ 4.5:1 combined fill + casing. |
| ☐ | **Run** an accessibility audit (e.g., axe‑core on the page) to ensure the canvas has appropriate ARIA labels and a fallback description. |

---

## 8. Example full style snippet (minimal)

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "satellite": {
      "type": "raster",
      "tiles": ["https://my.cdn/sat/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpg"],
      "tileSize": 256
    },
    "openmaptiles": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "https://my.cdn/tiles.json"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    { "id": "background", "type": "background", "paint": { "background-color": "#000000" } },

    // 1️⃣ Satellite imagery
    { "id": "satellite", "type": "raster", "source": "satellite" },

    // 2️⃣ (optional) hillshade here …

    // 3️⃣ Terrain fills (land, water, parks) …
    // 4️⃣ Road fills
    {
      "id": "road-fill",
      "type": "line",
      "source": "openmaptiles",
      "source-layer": "transportation",
      "filter": ["!=", "class", "path"],
      "layout": { "line-cap": "round", "line-join": "round" },
      "paint": {
        "line-color": [
          "match",
          ["get", "class"],
          "motorway", "#e0e0e0",
          "primary", "#c8c8c8",
          "secondary", "#b8b8b8",
          "tertiary", "#b0b0b0",
          "residential", "#f0f0f0",
          "#d8d8d8"   // default
        ],
        "line-width": [
          "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
          5, 0.5,
          10, 2,
          14, 6,
          18, 12
        ]
      }
    },
    // 5️⃣ Road casings (drawn after fill)
    {
      "id": "road-casing",
      "type": "line",
      "source": "openmaptiles",
      "source-layer": "transportation",
      "filter": ["!=", "class", "path"],
      "layout": { "line-cap": "round", "line-join": "round" },
      "paint": {
        "line-color": [
          "match",
          ["get", "class"],
          "motorway", "#5a5a5a",
          "primary", "#4a4a4a",
          "secondary", "#3a3a3a",
          "tertiary", "#3a3a3a",
          "residential", "#6a6a6a",
          "#5a5a5a"
        ],
        "line-width": [
          "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
          5, 1,
          10, 4,
          14, 8,
          18, 14
        ]
      }
    },

    // 6️⃣ Other vector layers (boundaries, rivers, …)

    // 7️⃣ Basemap label symbols (keep them on top)
    // (these come from the OSM‑Bright style or your own label layers)

    // 8️⃣ Your custom data layers (insert before the first symbol if you need them under labels)
  ]
}
```

Replace the `tiles` URLs with your own sources, and adjust the `match` statements if you have additional road classes (e.g., `service`, `track`, `path`). The key point is **no opacity**, **muted greys**, **casing darker than fill**, and **proper layer order**.

---

### TL;DR

* **Do not** lower road opacity.  
* **Desaturate** the road
